A disease model says how infectious people are; the mixing says who meets whom, and how often. This page covers the ways of giving the mixing in Starsim: homogeneous mixing, mixing pools, and networks of individual contacts (random, sexual, mother-to-child, and household networks). Contact matrices between groups, such as age groups, are in [Population data](populations_data.qmd), and several places with movement between them in [Geography](populations_geography.qmd). The tutorial [A2 – Networks](../tutorials/a2_networks.qmd) builds up the same material as a single worked path, and [T4 – Age groups and contacts](../tutorials/t4_ages.qmd) uses a contact matrix in a compartmental model.

## Choosing how people mix

The disease and the mixing are separate: changing from homogeneous mixing to a network does not change the disease. Each way of mixing is a **route** (a path by which infection can pass), given to the sim with `networks=`, which takes networks and mixing pools alike, singly or as a list:

- **No route given**: homogeneous mixing, the assumption of the standard ODE models. Everyone is equally likely to meet everyone else, and the transmission rate β (`beta`) is a rate per unit time: in `S >> I @ beta*I`, each susceptible person is infected at a rate of β times the share of people who are infectious.
- **A mixing pool**, `ss.MixingPool(n_contacts=10)`: homogeneous mixing with 10 contacts per unit time. β is then the probability that a contact with an infectious person infects, so β × the number of contacts is the transmission rate.
- **A contact matrix**, `ss.contacts(...)`: mixing between groups, such as age groups, with a number of contacts for each pair of groups (see [Population data](populations_data.qmd)).
- **A network**, such as `ss.RandomNet(n_contacts=10)` or `ss.SexualNet()`: contacts between particular people, with β per contact (or per sex act, on a network with acts).

Here is the same disease under three kinds of mixing. With no route, β = 0.05 per day and an infectious period of 10 days give R0 = β × the infectious period = 0.5, so there is no epidemic. With 10 contacts a day, R0 = 0.05 × 10 × 10 = 5, and the mixing pool and the random network give nearly the same epidemic:

```{python}
import starsim as ss
import starsim.library as ssl

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
infection = S >> I @ 0.05*I       # β = 0.05: per day with no route, per contact with one
recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(10)  # Infectious for 10 days on average
sir = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_prev=0.01)

kw = dict(n_agents=10_000, stop=ss.days(120), verbose=0)
scenarios = {
    'Homogeneous mixing':    ss.Sim(sir, **kw),
    'Mixing pool (10 contacts a day)': ss.Sim(sir, networks=ss.MixingPool(n_contacts=10), **kw),
    'Random network (10 contacts a day)': ss.Sim(sir, networks=ss.RandomNet(n_contacts=10), **kw),
}
msim = ss.parallel(scenarios)
msim.plot('sir.I')
```

Transmission along every route is frequency-dependent: a person's number of contacts is fixed, and what matters is the share of them who are infectious. This is the usual assumption for infections passed directly between people. A density-dependent rate, which grows with the number of people infected rather than their share, is written with the count itself, `S >> I @ ss.perday(3e-5)*I.n` (see [Diseases](building_diseases.qmd)).

### Which solver runs it

A model whose mixing has a compartmental form (no route, a mixing pool, or a contact matrix) runs as an ODE unless it is given agents, as the first and second sims above would without `n_agents`. A network is about particular people, so a model with a network runs as agents. A compartmental solver can still be asked for (`solver='ode'`); it then approximates the network, and says so in one line:

| Route | As agents | As compartments |
|---|---|---|
| none given | exact | exact |
| `ss.MixingPool(n_contacts=c)` | exact | exact |
| `ss.MixingPools(...)`, `ss.contacts(...)` | exact | exact |
| `ss.RandomNet(n_contacts=c)` | exact | homogeneous mixing with `c` contacts per unit time |
| `ssl.StaticNet(graph=...)` | exact | homogeneous mixing with the graph's mean number of contacts |
| `ss.DegreeNet()`, `ss.SexualNet()`, and other partnership networks | exact | the partner-change model (partnerships formed at a rate, each with the chance it transmits over its whole length), which needs the model stratified by sex for `ss.SexualNet` |

The approximations are rough where the network matters most: homogeneous mixing with the same mean number of contacts loses the variation between people, and the partner-change model counts at most one transmission in each partnership. [Solvers and backends](running_solvers.qmd) has the details. Anything that needs to know who a person's contacts are (contact tracing, partner notification, the transmission tree) needs a network, and so agents.

## Random networks

`ss.RandomNet` pairs people at random, with `n_contacts` contacts per person (a number, or a distribution such as `ss.poisson(lam=5)`). By default the contacts are redrawn every step. `dur=` makes them last, `dynamic=False` makes them once at the start and keeps them (people born or added later get none), and `age_range=[20, 65]` restricts the network to people of those ages. Several networks can be given together, each with its own name, as a layered population: here contacts at home (fully connected households of about three people, `ssl.ClusterNet`) and contacts at work among adults:

```{python}
households = ssl.ClusterNet(name='households', cluster_size=ss.poisson(3))
work = ss.RandomNet(name='work', n_contacts=10, age_range=[20, 65], dynamic=False)

S, I = ss.states('S I')
infection = S >> I @ 0.02*I       # Per contact, per day
recovery  = I >> S @ ss.days(10)  # No lasting immunity
sis = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_prev=0.01)

def make_sim(networks):
    return ss.Sim(sis, networks=networks, n_agents=2000, stop=ss.days(200), verbose=0)

msim = ss.parallel({'Work only': make_sim(work), 'Households and work': make_sim([households, work])})
msim.plot('sis.I')
print('Number of households:', msim.sims[1].networks.households.n_clusters)
```

Adding households raises the number infected at the endemic level: they reach children and older people, who have no contacts at work, and give each person a few more contacts. Each network's transmission is counted separately, so the same β applies on every layer unless it is given by route (see below).

`ssl.HybridNet` gives the four layers of [Covasim](https://covasim.org/) in one: households (`h`), schools (`s`), and workplaces (`w`), each a `ssl.ClusterNet` limited by age where it should be, and the community (`c`), a random network. Once in a sim, it becomes four networks, each reached (and changed) on its own, e.g. `sim.networks.s`; a `dt`, `start`, or `stop` given to it is passed to all four:

```{python}
hybrid = ss.Sim(sis, networks=ssl.HybridNet(household_size=3), n_agents=2000, stop=ss.days(100), verbose=0)
hybrid.run()
for net in hybrid.networks():
    print(net.label, 'edges:', len(net))
```

## Sexual networks

`ss.SexualNet` is a network of partnerships between two groups of people: by default a man and a woman, or two men (`between='mm'`), or any two groups by name, such as female sex workers and their clients (`between=('fsw', 'client')`). A partnership lasts `dur`, and has `acts` sex acts per unit time. Partnerships and acts are separate numbers, with separate sources of data (numbers of partners from surveys, how long partnerships last, how often partners have sex), so that a probability of transmission per act means what it says.

By default, people with no partner are paired on every step, so nobody has more than one partner at a time. With `n_contacts=`, the mean number of partners at a time is a target instead, and so are `concurrency=` (the share with two or more), `max_contacts=`, and `match=` (the share of partnerships between people at the same level of a property, e.g. `match=dict(risk=0.8)`). People then look for partners at the rates that make those targets the network's stable state. `net.check()` runs the sim again (three times by default) and compares the network it makes with each target:

```{python}
net = ss.SexualNet(n_contacts=1.2, concurrency=0.1, dur=ss.years(2))
sim = ss.Sim(n_agents=2000, networks=net, start=2000, stop=2010, dt=ss.months(1), verbose=0)
sim.run()
sim.networks.sexualnet.check(output=True)
```

`ss.SexualNet` is `ss.DegreeNet` between men and women, with an age of debut and participation. Partnerships that are not sexual, such as needle sharing among people who inject drugs, are `ss.DegreeNet` itself, which takes the same targets among anyone (or the people that `where=` gives, or between two groups with `between=`), with a target of one partner each by default.

## Transmission that differs by route

Infectiousness belongs to the disease, and contact to the routes, but how infectious someone is can itself depend on the route: HIV passes far more readily through a shared needle than through sex, and more readily from men to women than the reverse. The disease then gives one β for each route, as a dict keyed by the route's name (the network's class in lowercase, unless it was given a `name=`). On a network with directions, β takes a value for each: `ss.peract(m2f=..., f2m=...)` is a probability per act from men to women and from women to men. Every route needs a value, so that none is left out by mistake.

Here an infection passes through a random network of social contacts and through a sexual network:

```{python}
S, I = ss.states('S I')
beta = dict(randomnet=ss.peryear(0.2), sexualnet=ss.peract(m2f=0.01, f2m=0.005))
infection = S >> I @ beta*I
recovery  = I >> S @ ss.years(1)
sis = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_prev=0.05)

sim = ss.Sim(sis, networks=[ss.RandomNet(), ss.SexualNet()], n_agents=2000, start=2000, stop=2020, dt=ss.months(1), verbose=0)
sim.run()
sim.plot('sis')
```

## Mother-to-child networks

Transmission from mother to child needs pregnancy (`ss.Pregnancy`), which adds and removes the edges between mother and child: `ss.PrenatalNet` while the child is in the womb, `ss.BreastfeedingNet` while the mother breastfeeds, and `ss.PostnatalNet` for a period after birth (`dur=`). Their direction is one way, from mother to child. Here a chronic infection (one with no recovery) passes through partnerships and to children before birth, with β a probability per contact on the prenatal network:

```{python}
S, I = ss.states('S I')
beta = dict(sexualnet=ss.peract(m2f=0.01, f2m=0.005), prenatalnet=0.3)
infection = S >> I @ beta*I
chronic = ss.Disease(infection, init_prev=0.1)

pregnancy = ss.Pregnancy(fertility_rate=ss.freqperyear(100)) # Births a year per 1,000 women
deaths = ss.Deaths(death_rate=ss.peryear(0.01))
sim = ss.Sim(chronic, networks=[ss.SexualNet(), ss.PrenatalNet()], demographics=[pregnancy, deaths],
             n_agents=2000, start=2000, stop=2020, dt=ss.months(1), verbose=0)
sim.run()
sim.plot('chronic')
```

See [Demographics](populations_demographics.qmd) for pregnancy and births.

## Mixing pools

A mixing pool is homogeneous mixing among a group of people: no individual contacts, but each person has an effective number of contacts in the pool (drawn once, from `n_contacts`, and kept for the whole run). With no groups, a pool is everyone, as in the first example on this page. `src=` and `dst=` restrict it to the people who can infect (the sources) and the people who can be infected (the destinations), so a pool can be one-way. Each is a condition on people, a function of the sim returning a boolean array or UIDs, or `ss.AgeGroup(low, high)`, which works out who is in an age group once for each step and so is faster when there are many pools:

```{python}
pool = ss.MixingPool(
    src = ss.AgeGroup(low=0, high=15),     # Children infect ...
    dst = ss.AgeGroup(low=15, high=None),  # ... adults, but not each other
    n_contacts = ss.poisson(lam=5),        # 5 contacts a day on average
)
S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
infection = S >> I @ 0.05*I
recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(10)
sir = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_prev=0.05)
sim = ss.Sim(sir, networks=pool, n_agents=5000, stop=ss.days(120), verbose=0)
sim.run()
sim.plot('sir')
```

Each person in a pool has an effective number of contacts, drawn once from `n_contacts`. On each step, the force of infection in the pool is the mean infectiousness of the sources (the share of them infectious, weighted by each one's `rel_trans`), and each susceptible destination has a hazard of β × that mean × their number of contacts × their `rel_sus`, so is infected in the step with probability 1 − exp(−hazard × dt). This is the term β × S × I/N of the ODE, applied to each person.

Of the 5,000 people, 250 start infected, and the epidemic goes no further than the adults whom children infect: it dies out once the infected children recover, since nobody infects children in this pool and adults infect nobody. `ss.MixingPools` (plural) is a set of pools between groups, with `src` and `dst` as dicts of groups and `n_contacts` as a matrix, sources by row and destinations by column. For mixing by age, the usual case, `ss.contacts()` makes the `ss.MixingPools` from a contact matrix and a stratified model gives results by group: see [Population data](populations_data.qmd).

In a declared disease, β belongs to the transmission, not to the pool: a pool's own `beta` must be left at its default of 1, and any other value raises an error that says to give it to the transmission instead (e.g. `dict(mixingpool=...)`).

## Working with edges

A network keeps its edges as arrays: `p1` (the first person in each edge), `p2` (the second), and `beta` (a multiplier for each edge, 1 by default), reached as `net.edges` or as `net['p1']`. `net.find_contacts(uids)` gives the contacts of some people, `net.to_df()` the edges as a table, and `net.remove_edges()` removes edges by index or by a boolean array. A network can also be made from a table of edges with `from_df()`:

```{python}
sim = ss.Sim(n_agents=1000, networks=ss.RandomNet(n_contacts=4), stop=ss.days(10), verbose=0)
sim.run()
net = sim.networks.randomnet
print('Edges:', len(net))
print('Contacts of person 0:', net.find_contacts([0]))

custom = ss.Network(name='custom').from_df(dict(p1=[0, 1, 2], p2=[1, 2, 3]))
custom.to_df()
```

Edges can be removed by a condition on them or by position, and `net.eligible()` gives the people who can form edges (alive, and within an age range if given), here on the community layer of the hybrid network above:

```{python}
net = hybrid.networks.c
print('Community edges:', len(net))
net.remove_edges(net['p1'] < 100) # Remove the edges whose first person has a UID below 100
net.remove_edges([0, 1, 2])       # Remove the first three edges
print('After removing some:', len(net))
print('People of school age:', net.eligible(age_range=[6, 22]).sum())
```

Changing the edges of a network in the middle of a run is the job of an intervention (see [Interventions](interventions_interventions.qmd)), such as closing schools; the edges of a network that is redrawn each step come back on the next step.

A network of partnerships forgets a partnership when it ends. With `memory=`, it keeps those that ended within that time, so that `net.find_contacts()`, and so contact tracing (the `trace=` of a delivery: see [Interventions](interventions_interventions.qmd)), also reaches recent past partners, as for partner notification of the past year's partners:

```{python}
net = ss.SexualNet(dur=ss.lognorm_ex(mean=ss.years(1), std=ss.years(1)), memory=ss.years(1))
sim = ss.Sim(n_agents=2000, networks=net, start=2000, stop=2005, dt=ss.months(1), verbose=0)
sim.run()
net = sim.networks.sexualnet
uids = ss.uids(range(200))
print('Current partners of 200 people:', len(ss.Network.find_contacts(net, uids)))
print('Including those of the past year:', len(net.find_contacts(uids)))
```

## Networks available

| Network | What it is | Main parameters |
|---|---|---|
| `ss.RandomNet` | Contacts at random, redrawn each step or lasting | `n_contacts`, `dur`, `dynamic`, `age_range` |
| `ss.SexualNet` | Partnerships between two groups (men and women by default) | `between`, `dur`, `acts`, `debut`, `participation`, `n_contacts`, `concurrency`, `max_contacts`, `match`, `memory` |
| `ss.PrenatalNet` | Mother and unborn child, from `ss.Pregnancy` | none |
| `ss.BreastfeedingNet` | Mother and child while she breastfeeds, from `ss.Pregnancy` | none |
| `ss.PostnatalNet` | Mother and child after birth | `dur` |
| `ss.MixingPool` | Homogeneous mixing within a group, or from one group to another | `src`, `dst`, `n_contacts` |
| `ss.MixingPools` | Mixing between several groups | `src`, `dst`, `n_contacts` (a matrix) |
| `ss.contacts()` | A contact matrix (returns `ss.MixingPools`) | see [Population data](populations_data.qmd) |

The library (`import starsim.library as ssl`) has more:

| Network | What it is | Main parameters |
|---|---|---|
| `ssl.ClusterNet` | Fully connected clusters, such as households | `cluster_size`, `dynamic`, `age_range` |
| `ssl.HybridNet` | Households, schools, workplaces, and community, as in Covasim | `household_size`, `contacts`, `school_ages`, `work_ages`, `clustered` |
| `ssl.StaticNet` | A fixed network from a NetworkX graph | `graph`, `p`, `n_contacts` |
| `ssl.ErdosRenyiNet` | Each pair of people connected with a probability | `p`, `dur` |
| `ssl.DiskNet` | People who move in a plane, in contact within a radius | `r`, `v` |
| `ssl.RandomSafeNet` | A random network whose draws keep scenario comparisons free of chance differences | `n_edges`, `dur` |
| `ssl.NullNet` | No contacts, for testing | none |

## Writing a network

A network written as code is a subclass of one of these (usually `ss.DynamicNetwork`, for partnerships that form and end, or `ss.SexualNet`) that overrides how edges are made. The methods it can override:

| Method | What it does |
|---|---|
| `add_pairs()` | Makes new edges; the main method to override |
| `remove_pairs()` | Ends edges, e.g. those whose duration is over |
| `step()` | Called every step; by default removes, then adds, pairs |
| `init_post()` | Sets the network up once the people exist |
| `find_contacts()` | Gives the contacts of some people |

[Custom modules](building_modules.qmd) has the general pattern, including parameters, states, and results of a module's own, and the tutorial [A5 – Custom modules](../tutorials/a5_modules.qmd) writes a network step by step.

## Pitfalls

- **β changes meaning when a route is added.** With no route, β is a rate per unit time; with a mixing pool, contact matrix, or network, it is a probability per contact (per act, on a network with acts). Adding `networks=ss.RandomNet(n_contacts=10)` to a model fitted with homogeneous mixing multiplies its R0 by 10, as in the first example on this page.
- **A network makes the model agent-based.** Asking for `solver='ode'` with a network approximates it; check the note it prints, and [Solvers and backends](running_solvers.qmd) for how far the approximation goes.
- **A probability per act needs acts.** `ss.peract()` on a route without acts (a random network, a mixing pool, a mother-to-child network) raises an error; give a bare probability per contact instead.
- **A β by route names every route.** A dict that leaves out a route, or names one that isn't in the sim, raises an error that lists the routes there are.
- **A static network leaves out newcomers.** With `dynamic=False`, edges are made once, and people born or added later have no contacts on that network.

The API reference for this page: [Networks](../api/networks.qmd).

## Further reading

- [EpiModel: Network models](https://epimodel.github.io/EpiModel/articles/Intro.html): stochastic network models of HIV and other STIs, estimated with exponential random graph models
- [Covasim: Population structures](https://docs.covasim.org/tutorials/tut_people.html): the households, schools, workplaces, and community that `ssl.HybridNet` copies
- [NetworkX: Graph generators](https://networkx.org/documentation/stable/reference/generators.html): ready-made graphs that `ssl.StaticNet` can use
- [Mesa: Discrete space](https://mesa.readthedocs.io/latest/apis/discrete_space.html): agents placed on the cells of a grid or the nodes of a network
